revised_comments: Mozambique scored 66.07 out of 100 on the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI) 2024, placing it in the 'Advancing' tier and making it the top-ranked Portuguese-speaking African (PALOP) country in the index. This is a substantial improvement from a score of 24.18 in the 2020 edition, attributed to new cybersecurity legislation, clearer national plans and capacity-building initiatives, though the report notes continued gaps in societal cybersecurity awareness.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The cited DLA Piper source was fetched and, while it still confirms Mozambique has no general data protection law, the same page (last modified 17 February 2026) now also lists two new decrees — 71/2025 and 72/2025, both of 31 December 2025 — that were not reflected in the original score of 1. These establish sectoral data-location and sovereignty requirements, so the score is raised to 3.
revised_comments: Mozambique does not have comprehensive personal data protection legislation, but Decree No. 71/2025 (Data Centres Regulation) and Decree No. 72/2025 (Cloud Computing Regulation), both dated 31 December 2025, establish a licensing and governance framework for data centres and cloud services, applying extraterritorially to foreign providers serving Mozambican clients. The regulations impose specific location, security and technological-sovereignty requirements for data centres based abroad and for information classified as a state secret, together with sector-specific rules covering financial data. The framework entered into force on 31 March 2026 after a 90-day vacatio legis period, with a further one-year transition for existing operators to comply.

Definition: Frequency and severity of power outages experienced by businesses and households. Based on World Bank Enterprise Surveys, Afrobarometer, or national utility data. Reflects the quality of electricity supply beyond mere access — critical for running ICT equipment and data infrastructure.
Value Name: Severe (frequent daily outages or regular load shedding)
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The cited CGD source (2018 IVR phone survey covering 12 countries, not Mozambique-specific data) was fetched and only supports a general regional finding that 'daily outages are the norm almost everywhere', which is weaker evidence than the original score implies. The World Bank's formal Mozambique Enterprise Survey (2018) records a materially different picture — an average of 1.6 outages per month — which would sit closer to 'Moderate' (code 3) on this scale. Extensive 2024-2026 reporting also documents severe cyclone- and drought-driven disruption to the grid. Because the formal comparable metric (moderate) conflicts with the severe qualitative picture from recent climate-driven events, and no updated systematic outage-frequency survey exists, this is flagged for human review rather than asserting a code.
revised_comments: Evidence on Mozambique's grid reliability is mixed. The World Bank Enterprise Survey (2018) recorded firms experiencing an average of 1.6 power outages per month, consistent with a moderate rather than severe outage frequency. However, subsequent reporting describes recurrent severe disruption from cyclones (Chido, Dikeledi and Jude in the 2024-25 season alone affected hundreds of thousands of customers), a hydrological drought that cut national electricity production by around 25% in 2025, and infrastructure damage linked to civil unrest, all straining the state utility EDM's ability to maintain a reliable supply. No updated systematic outage-frequency survey has been identified since 2018.

Definition: The gap between men and women in mobile internet usage or internet access. Based on the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap data or ITU gender-disaggregated ICT statistics. A smaller gap indicates more equitable access to digital opportunities.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light check surfaced GSMA country-level survey data for Mozambique, so the row was moved to the full path. GSMA's 2018 consumer survey (published in its 2019 Africa report) gives a specific, large mobile-internet gender gap for Mozambique (~59%, code 1). This is the only Mozambique-specific figure found despite additional searching, and it is seven years old against a backdrop of regional narrowing (Sub-Saharan Africa's gap fell from 36% in 2022 to 29% in 2024 per GSMA), so the score is raised from 0 to 1 but flagged for human review to obtain a fresher country estimate.
revised_comments: GSMA Intelligence's 2018 consumer survey found a very large gender gap in mobile internet use in Mozambique: around 9% of women used mobile internet compared with 22% of men, a gap of roughly 59 percentage points, alongside a mobile phone ownership gender gap of around 24%, then the third-largest among the markets GSMA surveyed. Mozambique's National Institute of Statistics has since begun publishing sex-disaggregated ICT data through the national census, which could support a more current assessment, though no more recent country-specific gender-gap figure has been identified. The regional Sub-Saharan Africa mobile internet gender gap has narrowed markedly since (from around 36% in 2022 to 29% in 2024 per GSMA), suggesting Mozambique's gap may since have narrowed as well.
